strategies.name: Protect the soil
strategies.subtitle: Cereal rye before soybeans, rye again before corn

why.text: Cereal rye is one of the most popular cover crops planted before soybeans.
Rye gives some of the strongest erosion protection through fall and winter.

evidence.text: If low soil moisture is a concern, NC State suggests ending the cover at least two weeks before soybean planting.
Each spring since 1981 replayed with NASA rainfall for this location.

benefits.text: Can suppress weeds and, with no-till, help conserve soil moisture later in the season.
Small grains can be planted after soybean harvest, so the second winter is covered too.

gaps.text: Actual rye growth and residue depend on your field and are not measured here.
A moisture rule for corn planting after a cover crop has not been sourced yet.

risks.text: A living cover uses soil moisture. In a dry spring it can leave the seedbed too dry.
Grass covers can tie up soil nitrogen as they break down, which matters before corn.
Extra seed, planting and termination work.

strategies.name: Earn more
strategies.subtitle: Wheat for grain, then June soybeans

why.text: Adds a third crop to sell from the same land over two years.

evidence.text: NC State reports lower yields for soybeans planted in June than in the Apr 20–May 20 window.
Each June planting window since 1981 replayed with NASA rainfall.

benefits.text: Grain income from the wheat crop.
Wheat covers the soil through the first winter.

gaps.text: Wheat planting and harvest dates are sample values until an NC State small-grain source is linked.
Prices and costs are not included.

risks.text: A dry seedbed right after wheat harvest.
Little time between wheat harvest and soybean planting.
